title: Standing waves and resonance; Doppler effect
source: Questions and terms copied unchanged from the site's bank, except where marked for IB Diploma Physics (status of the source: ai-reviewed-reverified-gate-verified-2026-09-29-awaiting-human-signoff). Terms and clues: C.4#c05 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; C.4#c20 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; C.4#c19 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition; C.4#c15 bank term, first sentence of the bank's definition. assemble.prompt: Match each term to its definition.

items.label: Antinode (displacement antinode)
items.clue: A point on a standing wave at which the amplitude of oscillation is greatest.

items.label: Critical damping
items.clue: The smallest degree of damping at which a displaced system returns to equilibrium without oscillating.

items.label: Light damping
items.clue: Damping small enough that the displaced system oscillates about equilibrium with an amplitude that decreases gradually over many cycles.

items.label: Resonance
items.clue: The large increase in the amplitude of a forced oscillation that occurs when the driving frequency equals (for a lightly damped system, very nearly equals) a natural frequency of the system.

questions.stem: Which statement about a standing wave on a string is correct?

options.text: It forms where two identical waves travelling in opposite directions superpose.
It is a single wave that has stopped travelling, so its crests stay in fixed places.
It carries energy along the string from the source towards the far end.
Each point oscillates slightly later than its neighbour nearer the source.

questions.explanation: A standing wave is the superposition of two waves with the same frequency, wavelength, amplitude and speed moving in opposite directions, on a string usually the incident wave and its reflection. Their displacements add at every point, producing fixed nodes and antinodes.

questions.stem: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in a standing wave. Its nodes are at x = 0, 0.40 m, 0.80 m and 1.20 m, measured from one end. Points P, Q and R on the string are at x = 0.10 m, 0.20 m and 0.70 m. Which statement about the oscillations of P, Q and R is correct?

options.text: P and Q oscillate π/4 rad out of phase, being λ/8 apart.
P and Q oscillate in phase, with amplitudes equal to each other.
P and R oscillate in antiphase, with equal amplitudes.
P and R oscillate in phase, with equal amplitudes.

questions.stem: A pipe is closed at one end and open at the other. The air in the pipe vibrates in its first harmonic. Where along the pipe is the displacement of the air zero at all times?

options.text: At the closed end of the pipe
Midway between the two ends
At both ends of the pipe
At no point along the pipe

questions.stem: A lightly damped mass–spring system has a natural frequency of 2.0 Hz. It is driven by a periodic force of constant amplitude with a frequency of 3.5 Hz. Which describes its oscillation once the amplitude has become steady?

options.text: At 3.5 Hz, with a smaller amplitude than when driven at 2.0 Hz
At 2.0 Hz, its natural frequency, with a small steady amplitude
At 3.5 Hz, with a larger amplitude than when it is driven at 2.0 Hz
At 3.5 Hz, with the same amplitude as when it is driven at 2.0 Hz

questions.explanation: In the steady state a forced oscillator moves at the driving frequency, 3.5 Hz. The amplitude is greatest when the driving frequency is close to the natural frequency (2.0 Hz, resonance) and smaller away from it.

questions.stem: A lightly damped oscillator is driven by a periodic force of constant amplitude, and its steady amplitude is measured over a range of driving frequencies. The damping is then increased slightly, and the measurements are repeated. Which describes the new response curve compared with the first?

options.text: The maximum amplitude decreases, and it occurs at a slightly higher frequency.
The maximum amplitude decreases, and it occurs at a slightly lower frequency.
The maximum amplitude is unchanged, and it occurs at the same frequency.
The amplitude falls by the same factor at every frequency; the peak frequency is unchanged.

questions.stem: A mass–spring system is displaced from equilibrium and released. Which statement about the effect of damping on its motion is correct?

options.text: Heavy damping: no oscillation, but a slower return to equilibrium than with critical damping.
Heavy damping: no oscillation, and a quicker return to equilibrium than with critical damping.
Critical damping: it passes through equilibrium once, then comes to rest at equilibrium.
Light damping: the time period decreases steadily as the amplitude of oscillation decreases.

questions.stem: A loudspeaker on a trolley emits sound of constant frequency. The trolley moves at constant velocity along a straight track directly towards a stationary microphone, and has not yet reached it. How does the frequency detected by the microphone compare with the emitted frequency while the trolley approaches?

options.text: It is higher, and it rises steadily as the trolley gets nearer.
It is the same; only the loudness of the sound increases.
It is the same, because the source alone sets the frequency.
It is higher, and it stays constant while the velocity is constant.

questions.stem: A wavefront diagram shows the sound from a source moving at constant speed through still air towards a stationary observer X. Each wavefront is drawn as a circle centred on the point where the source was when that wavefront was emitted. Compared with the waves the same source emits when it is at rest, how do the waves reaching X differ?

options.text: An unchanged wavelength, and a greater speed through the air
A shorter wavelength, and the same speed through the air
A shorter wavelength, and a greater speed through the air
An unchanged wavelength, and the same speed through the air

questions.stem: A spectral line of hydrogen has a wavelength of 656.3 nm when measured in the laboratory. A galaxy is moving directly away from Earth at 3.00 × 10⁶ m s⁻¹. Take c = 3.00 × 10⁸ m s⁻¹. At what wavelength is this line observed in the spectrum of the galaxy?
questions.explanation: v/c = (3.00 × 10⁶)/(3.00 × 10⁸) = 0.0100, much less than 1, so Δλ/λ ≈ v/c applies: Δλ = 0.0100 × 656.3 nm = 6.563 nm. The galaxy is receding, so the line is redshifted to a longer wavelength: 656.3 + 6.563 = 662.9 nm.

questions.stem: Every absorption line in the spectrum of a star in our galaxy is at a slightly longer wavelength than the same line measured in the laboratory. What does this show about the star?

options.text: It is moving towards Earth.
It is a cool, red-looking star.
It is moving away from Earth.
It is a very long way from Earth.

questions.explanation: A longer wavelength for every line (a redshift) means the wavefronts reaching Earth are more widely spaced than those emitted, which happens when the source moves away. The fractional shift Δλ/λ ≈ v/c gives the star's speed along the line of sight.

questions.stem: A string fixed at both ends vibrates in its first harmonic. At one instant every point on the string has zero displacement, so the string is straight. Which statement about the string at this instant is correct?

options.text: Every point is momentarily at rest; its energy is all stored as elastic potential energy.
The two waves have cancelled each other out, so the string holds no energy at this instant.
Energy is being carried along the string from one fixed end to the other.
Points between the ends are moving at their greatest speeds; its energy is all kinetic.

questions.stem: A vibrator of frequency 320 Hz sets up a standing wave on a stretched string. The distance between adjacent nodes is 0.45 m. What is the speed of the travelling waves on the string?

options.text: 144 m s⁻¹
288 m s⁻¹
576 m s⁻¹
356 m s⁻¹

questions.explanation: Adjacent nodes are half a wavelength apart, so λ = 2 × 0.45 = 0.90 m. v = fλ = 320 × 0.90 = 288 m s⁻¹.

questions.stem: A train approaches a stationary observer at a constant speed of 40.0 m s⁻¹ while sounding a horn of frequency 800 Hz. The speed of sound in the air is 340 m s⁻¹. What frequency does the observer hear?

options.text: 716 Hz
907 Hz
894 Hz
800 Hz

questions.explanation: The source approaches, so the wavefronts ahead of it are crowded and the frequency rises: f′ = f(v/(v − u_s)) = 800 × 340/(340 − 40.0) = 800 × 340/300 = 907 Hz.

questions.stem: A dipper vibrating at 4.0 Hz makes water waves that travel across a tank at 0.80 m s⁻¹. A small model boat moves directly away from the stationary dipper at a constant speed of 0.20 m s⁻¹ through the still water. At what frequency does the boat meet the wavefronts?

options.text: 5.0 Hz
3.2 Hz
3.0 Hz
4.0 Hz

questions.explanation: The dipper is at rest, so the wavelength is unchanged: λ = 0.80/4.0 = 0.20 m. The boat moves away, so the wavefronts pass it at v − u_o: f′ = f((v − u_o)/v) = 4.0 × 0.60/0.80 = 3.0 Hz, which is 0.60 m s⁻¹ ÷ 0.20 m.

questions.stem: A test vehicle moves at constant velocity along a straight track and carries a siren that emits sound of frequency 500 Hz. A stationary microphone on the line of the track, beyond one end of it, detects the sound at 450 Hz. The speed of sound is 340 m s⁻¹. Taking velocity away from the microphone as positive, what is the velocity of the vehicle?
